content.title: Reply to the reviewer
content.comment:
Thanks for the comments and feedback.

1. Relation to Shapley value: thanks for pointing out this connection. Indeed Shapley value, and more generally the direction of “data valuation” which estimates the value of training examples is closely related to the algorithm used to estimate counterfactual memorization and influence used in this paper. This topic goes all the way back to leave-one-out error estimation. We will add a paragraph to discuss this in the related work. The main difference between the research on data valuation and this paper is that the former focus on better estimators and algorithms to compute the scores, while we focus on using the algorithm to estimate and analyze memorization / influence in real world neural language modeling tasks.

2. Question: “easy examples tend to have low memorization” does not hold for Wiki40k. We would like to clarify that the fact that Fig.1(Wiki40B) does not have points around the lower left corner does not contradict the conclusion. In fact, the main reason is that the easiest documents in Wiki40B are more difficult than the easiest documents in the other two datasets, because there are examples that contain short phrases, many spaces, and highly duplicated documents. While for Wiki40B, even the easiest document cannot reach extremely high per-token accuracy after training on it for many epochs.

content.title: Reply to the reviewer
content.comment:
Thanks to the reviewer for the feedback and comments.

1. We limit the training set size due to the computation complexity of the algorithm, because it is very costly to train even a single model at the largest scale. However, we argue that the analytical results carried out on a subset of training documents reflect the nature of the results well. The qualitative examples identified by this metric at different memorization ranges closely match the intuition behind counterfactual memorization. Regarding training epochs, as reported in Fig.4, the relative ranking is consistent between few and many epochs. 

2. The mathematical formulation is borrowed from Feldman & Zhang (2020), as stated above definition 2.1. We apply it to neural language models under the intuition of counterfactual memorization, and analyze it in common language datasets. We will revise the introduction to make this more explicit.

3. As above.

4. It is proven theoretically in Feldman (2019) under certain assumptions of the data distribution and the learning algorithm. It is not clear how things behave in practice. To the best of our knowledge, this work is the first to analyze the behaviors and implications in neural language modeling tasks.

content.title: Reply to the reviewer
content.comment:
Thanks to the reviewer for the feedback and comments.

The term “counterfactual” indeed means “changing” a “fact” in the knowledgebase. To change common knowledge such as “Paris is a city in France”, it potentially requires removing or negating a lot of training documents. But for very specific information encoded only in a very limited number of documents (e.g. a specific episode of event), removing or negating one training document is enough. We are actually utilizing this to distinguish examples that encode specific information (counterfactually memorized) and examples that contain common information also available in other examples. Therefore, we believe the usage of counterfactual in this scenario is proper.

Active learning is related to this topic. However, one key difference is that active learning aims at finding a subset of examples that help most with the model test accuracy. Here we are more interested in the influence of a specific training example on a specific test (or training) example, instead of the average performance across all test examples. The formulation is indeed more deeply related to DP, where the goal is to limit the contribution of each single training example. Those examples with high memorization identified in this paper are exactly the examples that DP algorithms would like to constrain.

Analyzing attention mechanisms is an interesting research direction. However, while attention enables analysis of language model behaviors within each example, the focus of this paper is to analyze memorization across different examples. 

We also tried to use log-likelihood instead of per-token accuracy as the metric. The overall pattern is similar but the numerical range of the scores are a bit more difficult to interpret than the accuracy which falls into [0, 1].

content.title: Reply to the reviewer
content.comment:
Thanks to the reviewer for the comments and for appreciating the importance of this direction. 

1. Regarding interpreting the memorization score. We found via qualitative analysis of the examples, that 0.15 is generally a good threshold above which the examples mostly contain unique memorized information. The extremely high memorization score (>0.5) could be mostly associated with outliers such as foreign text. The nature of such text depends on the quality and domain of the dataset. We provided more qualitative examples at different score ranges in the Appendix. The reason that the correlation in Fig. 6 looks noisy is because the heldout set is much smaller than the training set. As a result, there are many memorized examples in the training set that do not have a corresponding heldout example. For example, a training example might be describing a very specific episode of an event, but this is not covered in any heldout document. If we increase the size of heldout set by sampling fresh examples from the same underlying distribution, more memorized training examples will be able to match with their counterpart in the heldout set.

2. As stated above the definition, the mathematical formulation is borrowed from Feldman & Zhang (2020). We will revise the introduction to make this more explicit as well. However, we think the original term “memorization” coined in Feldman & Zhang (2020) is too general, and especially easily confused with verbatim textual matching memorization that has been widely studied in language models. So we prefer the alternative term “counterfactual memorization” in this context.

3. Thanks for pointing out missing references.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper empirically studies memorization in language models, which is defined as how a model’s predictions change if a particular sample is omitted during training. The authors call it “counterfactual memorization”. Then the authors use similar formulation to compute the counterfactual influence that estimates the influence of training examples on validation or generation examples. This paper consists of a lot of empirical analysis including the memorization distribution, how it evolves over training, the correlation between memorization and influence, etc.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
### Strengths

1. I find the memorization aspect of LMs very interesting and definitely worth more future research efforts. Studying memorization may be important for researchers to better understand the behaviour of LMs and its generalization. Therefore, I think this paper would be relevant to a lot of audiences.
2. The experiments are comprehensive and detailed.
3. The paper writing is very clear.


### Weaknesses

1. Even though I appreciate that the authors spent a great effort presenting a comprehensive set of experiments, I feel the results/observations in the paper are not very inspiring and useful. For example, several experiments show the memorization distribution – the memorization metric is from the authors’ own definition and I can’t perceive the absolute values well (e.g. memorization=0.2 means that the token prediction accuracy drops by 20% without the example, Is 20% a high or low number? What does it tell us? Does 0.2 memorization imply the example is important or not?). Basically, I can’t read much helpful info out from the memorization distribution and I am not sure what it implies since the memorization number itself lacks further interpretations. The most significant study is Figure 6 from my perspective since it tries to reason that memorization may imply the example’s influence on heldout data. However, the correlation is noisy and not very strong. Therefore, I fail to see further insightful meaning of the memorization defined in this paper and am not sure whether it is a proper memorization definition in the context.
2. The authors claim that they define “counterfactual memorization” in neural LMs but the method appears to be more like a direct application of the memorization definition in Feldman & Zhang (2020) to LMs. I feel it is kinda misleading that the paper proposes a new term “counterfactual memorization” which is actually the same equation in Feldman & Zhang (2020) where they call it “memorization”. In the current version I think the intro may overclaim the originality of the “counterfactual memorization”. 


### Other questions/suggestions:
Very relevant reference: Memorization Without Overfitting: Analyzing the Training Dynamics of Large Language Models

The paper is generally well-written and the experiments are comprehensive. 
 
I think it may be inaccurate to use the term ''counterfactual '' since the paper does not focus on detecting the incorrect or non-existing facts in the training set. ''counterfactual'' is so often popularly associated with introducing knowledge or logic rules into the language model.

Even though these ideas stem from other research fields, this paper contributes to the relevant topics in the NLP field. 
.  
How about to compare the proposed analysing method with the attention machnism, since the attention can also indicate which part is important in the language models. 
 
It would be better to try more measurements rather than only use per-token accuracy, since there are many other factors that may affect the next-token prediction.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper studies memorization in NLMs. The authors adopt the definition of memorization from Feldman & Zhang (2020) (i.e., the difference between quality when an example is present in training vs when it is not). The definition is taken as in the original paper studying classification, i.e. token-level accuracy (and not generation properties as would be more natural for the language modeling task). Under this definition, they consider a toy-task setting (overfitting on 2m training examples) and make several observations: (1) high memorization examples generally come from unconventional text, (2) different domains in the training set have different memorization levels, (3) for examples from both the validation set and the model generated texts, the model predictions could be drastically different depending on the presence or absence of a particular training example with high memorization.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:

1) The problem of memorization in large LMs is important

2) The work considers the notion of memorization different from previous works on privacy.

Weaknesses:

1) Despite what is claimed in the abstract/introduction/etc, the paper works in a toy-task setting instead of studying “modern language models”. Specifically, the paper (1) takes extremely small datasets of 2m examples and (2) overfits models on these datasets to increase memorization - this makes the setting artificial. Since important properties of modern LMs arise in a very different setting, it is not clear whether the results are valid for modern models. At the very least, this toy-tak artificial nature of the considered models has to be mentioned prominently throughout abstract, intro, contributions, conclusions, discussion, and all the results have to be viewed from this perspective. 

2) One of the main claimed contributions of the paper is the definition of the counterfactual memorization for LMs (abstract, contribution 1, etc). However, the paper took definition from Feldman & Zhang (2020) with no change: the considered memorization was for the token-level classification task. I don’t think this can be considered as a contribution.

3) Similarly, the notion of counterfactual influence mentioned in conclusions is also taken as-is from previous work.

4) One of the main conclusions was not only made in previous work, but proven theoretically in a more general case. Namely, one of the main conclusions made by the authors is “We found that for examples from both the validation set and the model generated texts, the model predictions could be drastically different depending on the presence or absence of a particular training example with high memorization.” - for natural datasets, this was proven to be generally the case (Feldman, 2019). In short, this was the main reason for concluding that memorization is a healthy part of model training (see “Does Learning Require Memorization? A Short Tale about a Long Tail”, Feldman, 2019).
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, while the research direction of the work is important, the paper in its current state is misleading in terms of (1) toy-task artificial nature of the models and hence outcomes of the analysis, (2) proposed methods and results (treating LMs as classification and hence resorting to what’s been done before, claiming as valuable observations something that has been proven theoretically to occur, etc).

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes to study the *counterfactual memorization* and *counterfactual influence* of training examples. Counterfactual memorization is defined as the difference between expected accuracies of an example when presenting in the training data and absent in the training data. Counterfactual influence is defined as the difference between expected accuracies of another example when an example is presenting in the training data and absent in the training data. They performed analysis on several data, and found that format is a good predictor of counterfactual memorization, and counterfactual influential data pairs are almost identical or about the same event.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:

1. The definition of counterfactual memorization and influence makes sense and the sampling approximation is tractable. 
2. The authors perform detailed analysis on the data. 

Weakness:

1. The definition of counterfactual influence seems to be related to Shapley value, which also calculated the performance difference with and without a data point, which neither cited or mentioned in the paper. Could authors clarify the connection and differences in the manuscript? 
2. Despite the detailed analysis, it is hard to draw conclusion from the results (some of the claims are even false given the results, see Questions). This leads to the questions, whether this method is useful and what are its typical use cases. Format and event's influence on the scores seem to be superficial. 

Questions: 

In Sec. 3.1 Figure 1 analysis, it seems to me the trend authors found, "From the 2D density plots, we find that easy examples tend to have low memorization.", doesn't hold for Wiki40k:en, which contradicts to the claim "
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: Yes. The writing of this paper is very clear, so it should be very easy to reproduce. The novelty is not too high given its similarity to Shapley value and other work on interpretability.
content.summary_of_the_review: This is a well-written paper defines the method for analyzing the importance of data points mathematically. However, it is hard to draw any useful conclusion from the results. The method makes sense, but too similar to existing ones.

content.title: Counterfactual Memorization in Neural Language Models
content.abstract: Modern neural language models widely used in tasks across NLP risk memorizing sensitive information from their training data. As models continue to scale up in parameters, training data, and compute, understanding memorization in language models is both important from a learning-theoretical point of view, and is practically crucial in real world applications. An open question in previous studies of memorization in language models is how to filter out "common" memorization. In fact, most memorization criteria strongly correlate with the number of occurrences in the training set, capturing "common" memorization such as familiar phrases, public knowledge or templated texts. In this paper, we provide a principled perspective inspired by a taxonomy of human memory in Psychology. From this perspective, we formulate a notion of counterfactual memorization, which characterizes how a model's predictions change if a particular document is omitted during training. We identify and study counterfactually-memorized training examples in standard text datasets. We further estimate the influence of each training example on the validation set and on generated texts, and show that this can provide direct evidence of the source of memorization at test time.
